output:
*Interview with Dr Casimir Vauthier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Thank you for waiting, Doctor. You have known the household a long time.

DR VAUTHIER: Thirty years, Inspector. Aurèle and I argued about Gounod over a bottle he could not afford, and we have been arguing ever since. I attended the family when they needed me. I attended his brother Jules in his last illness in 1889, which I would not wish on any man. So I am not a stranger in that house, and I am not sure I am a fair witness to it.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the evening, as you remember it.

DR VAUTHIER: We dined. Aurèle was in good voice, which in his case means he was in a cruel one. When the temple struck nine he made us all bring out our watches, as he does every year, and he told each of us what was wrong with ours. Mine was two minutes ahead of the bell. He said it was a watch that wished to be early for its own funeral. I laughed. Aurèle was always kinder to his friends' watches than to their opinions.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

DR VAUTHIER: Madame and I played piquet in the salon. Odile plays a hard game, and a harder piano, but I have never beaten her at cards. We were in the middle of a hand when the temple struck ten. I looked at the salon clock, which showed five minutes to ten, and I remarked on it to Madame. She did not look up. She said nothing to it, which is her way.

MATTHEY: Go on.

DR VAUTHIER: We played until a quarter to eleven by my watch. Then I went out to the hall to fetch my cigar case from my coat. Madame began to play the piano as I went out. When I came back, she stopped.

MATTHEY: Which piece was it?

DR VAUTHIER: Chopin. Odile plays nothing else well, and she plays him better than anyone in Neuchâtel. I do not pretend to know the opus.

MATTHEY: You have examined the body.

DR VAUTHIER: I have. The wound is at the back of the skull, struck from behind with something heavy and square-edged. I should think the mallet you have already found on the floor. A man struck so would not have known much about it. It would have been very quick, Inspector. I can say that with confidence, and I will say no more than that, because a physician who guesses at the rest is worth less than a clerk.

MATTHEY: Did you notice anything about the atelier?

DR VAUTHIER: Only the regulator on the wall, which had stopped. Aurèle's repeater was in his hand. I will not make a sentimental thing of it. But the regulator stopped with its master, and I think that is the truest thing anyone will say tonight.

MATTHEY: Is there anything you have not told me, Doctor?

DR VAUTHIER: Only that Aurèle would have been insufferable tonight, and that he would have enjoyed being so. He had waited four years for that repeater. He would have wanted to be the first to strike the new century, and he would have wanted you to hear him do it. Tempus fugit, as the Romans said, though they never had a repeater to tell them so.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Doctor. Please do not leave the town without telling the police post.

DR VAUTHIER: I am not going anywhere in this frost, Inspector. Nor, I think, is anyone.
